video_title: The Fed's Next Punch in the Mouth | Protect the Pile Episode 21 w/ Danielle DiMartino Booth
gist: Danielle DiMartino Booth (QI Research) argues Fed Chair Warsh's hawkish, task-force-driven reset will get tested the same way Powell's did in 2018 -- this time by a far larger and less transparent web of private credit, CLOs, and commercial real estate -- while separately flagging a specific accounting mechanism (mark-to-market gains on private AI stakes like Anthropic) that she says is inflating roughly 35% of tech earnings in a way that would 'make Enron blush,' alongside a broader critique that official labor and inflation data are structurally unreliable.

themes.theme: Fed reaction function and the 2018 precedent

insights.claim: Jerome Powell's tough February 2018 rhetoric about not backstopping markets was met by a credit-market response that spilled into equities, including a record 41 days without a single junk bond priced after the last one sold on Halloween 2018, culminating in the Christmas Eve 2018 selloff and a rapid Fed pivot within days.
insights.speaker: Danielle DiMartino Booth, guest
insights.so_what: A concrete historical template for how a hawkish Fed chair gets 'punched in the mouth': credit markets seize first, stocks lag, and the Fed reverses once forced -- a sequence worth watching for under Warsh.
insights.quote: you've always got a plan until you get punched in the mouth

insights.claim: Fed Chair Warsh will likely hold a firmer line than Powell did if tested only by a plain equity-market correction, but the real test will come from the interconnectedness of markets Powell never had to face -- specifically collateralized loan obligations, a $2 trillion private credit market, private equity, and commercial real estate.
insights.speaker: Danielle DiMartino Booth, guest
insights.so_what: Frames the real stress-test for Fed independence under Warsh as a private-credit/CRE event rather than a stock-market drawdown -- a different risk transmission channel than the one investors watched in 2018.

insights.claim: CLOs are structurally no healthier today than during the last cycle when they were concentrated on Japanese bank balance sheets -- they are simply larger -- while distressed office sales hit a decade high in 2025, and a wave of high-yield and CRE debt with roughly five-year maturities from 2021-2022 is coming due in a 2026-to-late-2027 refinancing window that was not underwritten for today's higher-rate environment.
insights.speaker: Danielle DiMartino Booth, guest
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific, dated maturity wall (2026-late 2027) in CRE and high-yield paper as a concrete catalyst window for credit stress to watch, rather than an open-ended macro worry.
insights.quote: we're talking about a 2026, late 2027 event for a lot of this paper

insights.claim: Persistent downside surprises in core inflation across the US, Germany, and Canada -- with even PPI coming in cooler than expected -- were not on Wall Street's radar, and reflect a 'mother of all margin squeezes' as businesses' pricing power fails to keep pace with costs, suggesting the real risk may be disinflation rather than the reflation the Fed is positioned to fight.
insights.speaker: Danielle DiMartino Booth, guest
insights.so_what: If disinflation, not inflation, turns out to be the dominant near-term risk, a hawkish Fed positioning against 'last year's war' could be a policy error -- worth watching core CPI/PPI prints for confirmation.
insights.quote: the Fed is fighting last year's war, and there's disinflationary winds blowing right now

insights.claim: Bankruptcies are up 50% versus pandemic-era levels according to LendingTree data, and a rising share of full-time job losses is being offset by workers taking a second job -- underlying labor-market softness that consumer-facing headline data has not fully captured.
insights.speaker: Danielle DiMartino Booth, guest
insights.so_what: A household-stress data point that argues for caution on consumer-discretionary exposure and supports the disinflation/labor-weakness thesis over the market's reflation narrative.

themes.theme: The expanding definition of 'too big to fail'

insights.claim: Multi-trillion-dollar asset managers, large private-equity direct lenders (citing a $35 billion loan made directly by a PE firm this year), and even the stock market itself (via the 401k system putting retirement risk on individual investors) now arguably qualify as 'too big to fail' -- a scope expansion well beyond the traditional banks targeted by 2008-era reforms.
insights.speaker: Danielle DiMartino Booth, guest
insights.so_what: Investors should recognize that systemic-risk backstops (implicit or explicit) may now extend to private credit and even equity markets broadly, changing the calculus for how policymakers might respond to a future shock.
insights.quote: if too big to fail was what it was in 2008 it's grown tentacles. It's become a monster with multiple heads

insights.claim: Insurance regulators, including in all 51 US jurisdictions, reportedly lack visibility into what is actually backing many life insurance and annuity policies when the underlying assets sit in offshore reinsurance vehicles, creating an opaque, hard-to-track pocket of systemic risk in a sector assumed to be safe.
insights.speaker: Danielle DiMartino Booth, guest
insights.so_what: A specific, under-the-radar risk area (offshore reinsurance backing consumer annuities/life policies) worth flagging for anyone assessing insurer counterparty risk or annuity product safety.

themes.theme: AI infrastructure earnings-quality and accounting mechanics

insights.claim: A post-Dodd-Frank accounting rule requires holders of stakes in private companies to continuously mark those stakes to the latest funding-round valuation, meaning that whenever any investor makes a new investment in a private AI company like Anthropic, every existing shareholder must mark up their own stake's value straight into net income right before reporting earnings -- a mechanism she estimates (per Financial Times-cited research) affects roughly 35% of tech earnings.
insights.speaker: Danielle DiMartino Booth, guest
insights.so_what: A specific, quantifiable earnings-quality distortion that investors should strip out when evaluating hyperscaler/tech earnings -- reported net income may substantially overstate genuine operating profitability.
insights.quote: they have found a way to manipulate earnings that would make, you know, if you were to bring back Enron and WorldCom and put them in a room they'd blush. But, they're not breaking any laws.

insights.claim: The dynamic underlying tech-sector earnings has shifted from a debate about cash flows a couple of years ago, to leverage more recently, to now an accounting-driven mark-up mechanic on private AI stakes -- each step making reported profitability progressively harder for outside analysts to interpret at face value.
insights.speaker: Danielle DiMartino Booth, guest
insights.so_what: Signals that each successive year of the AI capex cycle has introduced a new, harder-to-audit earnings-quality issue -- a reason for increasing skepticism toward headline hyperscaler profitability metrics.

insights.claim: The quarterly census of employment and wages -- which captures more than 95% of US employer headcounts as hard, clean data -- showed actual job losses in Q1, Q2, and Q3 of 2025 that were not reflected in the initial payrolls prints, but this ground-truth data only becomes available roughly 18 months after the fact, too late to inform real-time policy.
insights.speaker: Danielle DiMartino Booth, guest
insights.so_what: A specific, sourced critique of headline payrolls reliability -- investors relying on the first payrolls print for labor-market conclusions should discount it against this lagging but more accurate benchmark.

insights.claim: Since January 2023, of the 40 subsequent monthly payroll reports, only 11 were revised upward versus 29 revised downward, and none of the revisions have converged with the more accurate quarterly census figures -- indicating a persistent, one-directional overstatement bias in the initial payrolls print, not just noise.
insights.speaker: Danielle DiMartino Booth, guest
insights.so_what: A quantified, systematic overstatement bias in headline jobs data that traders and policymakers should adjust for when reacting to the initial monthly print.

insights.claim: Seasonal-adjustment models are so rigid that in March 2026 -- officially the hottest March on record in the US per NOAA -- the payrolls model still attributed a large block of no-shows to snow-related absences, a factual impossibility that illustrates how outdated modeling assumptions distort even recent labor data.
insights.speaker: Danielle DiMartino Booth, guest
insights.so_what: A vivid, concrete illustration of methodological rot in official labor statistics -- reinforces skepticism toward the headline payrolls print as a real-time policy input.

insights.claim: A tax-law change requiring anyone earning above a certain threshold via platforms like Venmo/PayPal to obtain an employer identification number has been misread by government business-formation statistics as a genuine boom in new business creation (e.g., from lawn-mowing or babysitting), inflating small-business formation data with what is actually just a reporting-threshold artifact.
insights.speaker: Danielle DiMartino Booth, guest
insights.so_what: A specific data-integrity flaw that could be inflating perceived small-business dynamism/entrepreneurship statistics used by policymakers and analysts.

insights.claim: Real-time, automated feeds of hiring/firing events and price changes at medium-to-large companies are technologically feasible today (with AI-assisted methodology) and would convert 'the most lagging of all economic indicators' -- payrolls and prices -- into near real-time data, fundamentally changing how markets and the Fed react to stale monthly releases.
insights.speaker: Danielle DiMartino Booth, guest
insights.so_what: If implemented, would remove much of the current information edge from trading around monthly data releases, since markets would already have real-time visibility rather than reacting to lagging prints.
insights.quote: you're not making policy through a rearview mirror anymore

insights.claim: A real-time 'trimmed mean' inflation measure -- using continuously updated daily pricing data (such as Truflation's 15 million-plus tracked prices) while excluding one-off distortions like a single carrier's price cut that competitors match -- would be a more accurate and feasible replacement for the Fed's current core PCE framework.
insights.speaker: Danielle DiMartino Booth, guest
insights.so_what: A concrete alternative-data-based inflation methodology that, if adopted by the Fed's inflation-frameworks task force, would change how quickly and accurately markets and policymakers can assess true price trends.

themes.theme: Fed governance, internal politics, and structural reform

insights.claim: Warsh's success in reshaping Fed policy through his five task forces (communications, balance sheet, data, productivity/jobs, inflation frameworks) hinges on whether he can overcome resistance from the career Washington-based Fed staff -- the 'MIT mafia' -- who control what is discussed and analyzed at FOMC meetings, which she views as his single biggest institutional obstacle.
insights.speaker: Danielle DiMartino Booth, guest
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific internal power structure (career staff economists, not just the Board) that determines whether any Fed policy-framework reform actually takes hold -- a factor to watch beyond public Board votes.
insights.quote: getting past that Fed staff was always going to be his greatest challenge

insights.claim: Jerome Powell, having pledged deference to Warsh and stayed silent, may end up being Warsh's greatest ally on the Federal Reserve Board, while the real institutional pushback is expected to come from the regional Federal Reserve Bank presidents defending their 12-district structure, evidenced by their coordinated public criticism of Warsh's communications task force right up until the FOMC blackout period began.
insights.speaker: Danielle DiMartino Booth, guest
insights.so_what: Suggests the locus of internal Fed resistance to reform will be the regional bank presidents rather than the Washington Board -- a specific group to monitor for institutional friction under Warsh.

insights.claim: Christopher Waller has argued that in a world of electronic payments, the Fed's 12-district structure -- created shortly after banks moved money by stagecoach -- is largely obsolete and could be consolidated, with several regional Fed banks (e.g., St. Louis, Kansas City, Cleveland, Minneapolis) effectively redundant.
insights.speaker: Danielle DiMartino Booth, guest
insights.so_what: A structural Fed-reform idea with real internal backing that, if pursued, would be a significant governance shakeup worth monitoring alongside Warsh's task forces.

insights.claim: Whether the Fed's balance sheet ends up larger or smaller as a share of GDP by the end of Warsh's term depends almost entirely on political variables outside his control -- who holds the Treasury Secretary role and the outcome of the 2028 election -- rather than his own stated intent to shrink it.
insights.speaker: Danielle DiMartino Booth, guest
insights.so_what: Reinforces that balance-sheet policy is ultimately a function of fiscal/political coordination (Fed-Treasury alignment), not a purely technocratic Fed decision -- a reason to track Treasury leadership as closely as Fed leadership.

insights.claim: Historically, Marriner Eccles is judged the Fed chair with the 'strongest constitution' for refusing to be removed by President Truman after his term as chair ended, remaining as a governor until the 1951 Treasury-Fed Accord legally separated the two institutions -- in contrast to William McChesney Martin, who 'blinked' and lowered rates after being physically intimidated by President Lyndon Johnson.
insights.speaker: Danielle DiMartino Booth, guest
insights.so_what: A historical reminder that Fed independence has been repeatedly tested and has not always held under direct political pressure -- relevant context for assessing how durable Warsh's stated independence will prove.
